title: Trump Pardons Over 1,000 January 6 Defendants and Commutes 14 Sentences
description_short: On Jan. 20, 2025, Trump pardoned more than 1,000 people charged in the Jan. 6 attack and commuted 14 sentences, CNN reported.
description_medium: CNN reported that Trump’s January 20, 2025 order pardoned more than 1,000 people charged in connection with the Capitol attack and commuted 14 other sentences, including sentences for Proud Boys and Oath Keepers leaders. The two forms of clemency had different effects. CNN’s article supports this January 6 action, not the title’s 1,840-plus aggregate or unrelated corruption pardons.
description_long: CNN reported that on January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump pardoned more than 1,000 people charged in connection with the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol and commuted the sentences of 14 others. CNN described the pardons as covering people convicted of offenses related to the attack, including defendants who assaulted police officers. Among those whose sentences were commuted were leaders or members of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers; CNN explained that commutation ended or reduced prison terms without being the same legal act as a pardon. NPR’s contemporaneous report similarly described pardons for roughly 1,500 defendants and 14 commutations. The resulting legal change was a large reduction or removal of federal punishment for people prosecuted over January 6. The linked CNN story supports that dated clemency action, but it does not substantiate the original row’s 1,840-plus lifetime total, claims about pardons for unrelated corruption convictions, or a transactional motive. This draft is limited to the January 20 action and does not infer why Trump granted clemency.
notes: The linked CNN report supports the January 20, 2025, clemency actions against January 6 defendants. It does not establish the supplied synopsis's later 1,840-plus aggregate, pardons of corruption-convicted officials, or transactional motive; those claims require a dated recipient ledger and case-level records.

title: Trump Administration Fired 20 Immigration Judges in February 2025
description_short: AP reported that the administration fired 20 immigration judges in February 2025, including 13 who had not yet been sworn in.
description_medium: The Associated Press reported that 20 immigration judges were fired in February 2025 without explanation, citing the president of the union representing federal workers. Thirteen had not yet been sworn in, five were assistant chief immigration judges, and two more had been dismissed in the preceding week. The AP report does not support the row’s claim of 200-plus February firings or its asserted court effects and motive.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on February 15, 2025, that the Trump administration had fired 20 immigration judges without explanation, citing Matthew Biggs, president of the union representing federal workers. Biggs said 13 of those dismissed had not yet been sworn in and five were assistant chief immigration judges; two other judges had been fired under similar circumstances in the prior week. AP reported that the Executive Office for Immigration Review oversaw roughly 700 judges and that the courts already faced a large backlog. This source supports a specific February staffing action and the union’s account of who was affected. It does not support the original title’s claim that more than 200 judges were fired in that month, nor the supplied allegations that hearings were dismissed, that the action violated civil-service law, or that it was designed to enable deportations without review. The cited New York Times URL in the original row is about inspectors general, not immigration judges. The replacement narrows the event to the AP-documented count and leaves consequences and motive open.
notes: Needs context: The linked Times report concerns inspectors general, not immigration judges, and does not substantiate the asserted judge count, case impacts or motive.
Proposed correction: Obtain a contemporaneous report or DOJ personnel and caseload records before retaining the firing count and consequences.

title: Trump Signed a 2025 Law Limiting Some IRA Wind and Solar Credits
description_short: The 2025 reconciliation law ended certain IRA wind and solar electricity credits for covered facilities placed in service after Dec. 31, 2027.
description_medium: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, amended the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-electricity production and investment credits. For covered wind and solar facilities, the law ends Sections 45Y and 48E credits for facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, subject to statutory rules. It did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit.
description_long: President Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the Internal Revenue Code’s clean-electricity production credit under Section 45Y and clean-electricity investment credit under Section 48E. The statute provides that these credits do not apply to covered wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, and includes separate transition rules concerning when construction begins. The change narrows the period in which some Inflation Reduction Act clean-electricity credits can be claimed; it is more precise to describe it as a statutory termination for covered facilities than as blanket rescission of all IRA tax credits. Reuters’ July 2025 reporting described broader investment uncertainty after subsidy changes, but the statute is the stronger source for which credits and facilities are affected. The supplied row does not identify a credit-by-credit inventory, and this draft does not claim that all solar, wind, battery, electric-vehicle or already-committed projects lost support. The legal text establishes the cutoff and scope; project-specific eligibility depends on statutory definitions and transition provisions.

title: Reuters: $TRUMP Buyers Spent an Estimated $148 Million to Qualify for a Dinner
description_short: Reuters estimated buyers spent $148 million on $TRUMP tokens to qualify for a May 2025 dinner with Trump; the amount was based on token holdings, not a proven direct payment.
description_medium: Reuters reported that 220 top holders of the $TRUMP memecoin attended a May 22, 2025, dinner at Trump’s private club. It estimated their qualifying holdings at $148 million, including more than $111 million among the top 25, citing Inca Digital. Blockchain analysis suggested more than half of attendees were likely outside the United States; wallet data did not establish their nationalities.
description_long: Reuters reported that 220 top holders of Donald Trump’s $TRUMP memecoin attended a black-tie dinner at his private club in Virginia on May 22, 2025. Citing crypto-intelligence firm Inca Digital, Reuters estimated that investors held about $148 million in the token to secure their places, with the top 25 holders accounting for more than $111 million. The highest-ranking holders also received a private reception with Trump, and the four largest holders received a limited-edition watch. Reuters said blockchain analysis suggested more than half of the attendees were likely based outside the United States. That estimate concerns likely location inferred from wallet analysis; it does not establish attendees’ citizenship or prove every wallet owner’s identity was known. Nor does the estimated market value of token holdings establish that $148 million was paid directly to Trump or a Trump-affiliated entity. This correction focuses on the later dinner and its qualification mechanism, the event covered by the linked Reuters article. It does not use that May report to support the separate January launch claim about anonymous foreign wallets or an SEC decision.

title: Pompeo Invoked an Emergency for $8.1 Billion in Arms Transfers to Three Countries
description_short: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo invoked an emergency to expedite 22 arms transfers worth about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Jordan.
description_medium: Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced on May 24, 2019, that he had made an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers totaling about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. He cited deterring Iran and building partner self-defense capacity. The action bypassed the ordinary congressional review period.
description_long: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed the State Department to complete immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. Pompeo put their combined value at approximately $8.1 billion and said the transfers were intended to deter Iranian aggression and strengthen partner self-defense. A contemporaneous CNN report explained that invoking the emergency allowed the administration to expedite the sales without the ordinary congressional review period. The event was broader than the original title’s two named recipients: Jordan was also included. These sources establish the procedural action, approximate total and stated rationale. They do not provide in the cited press statement a full transfer-by-transfer list of weapons and services, or document the outcome of every congressional response. The revised text states the three recipients and attributes the rationale to the administration without treating it as independently proven or implying every transfer was delivered.
notes: The linked statement page returned HTTP 403. The exact arms packages and values, the administration’s stated emergency basis, and subsequent congressional response are missing; these are needed to explain the decision’s scope and consequences.

Wave3 evidence resolution: The source does not establish all 22 transfers were ultimately delivered. The statement gives the administration’s rationale, not independent proof of urgency. The source summary does not enumerate every item or subsequent congressional action.

title: Trump Pardons Paul L. Behrens After Health-Care Fraud Conviction
description_short: The DOJ lists Trump’s Jan. 13, 2021 pardon of Paul L. Behrens, whose 2014 sentence followed two health-care fraud and two related false-statement counts.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records Trump’s January 13, 2021, pardon of Paul L. Behrens in the Middle District of Florida. It lists two counts of health-care fraud and two counts of false statements related to health-care matters, with a 24-month prison sentence and two years of supervised release imposed in 2014. The list gives no case narrative or pardon rationale.
description_long: The Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney lists Paul L. Behrens under January 13, 2021, among pardons granted by President Donald Trump. The table identifies the Middle District of Florida and records a May 19, 2014 sentence of 24 months’ imprisonment and two years of supervised release. It lists two counts of health-care fraud and two counts of making false statements related to health-care matters. These are the case facts the official clemency record supplies, and they support a concise description of the conviction and pardon. The table does not describe the underlying health-care scheme, identify affected patients or payers, state the amount of loss, explain why Trump granted clemency, or report consequences after the pardon. Those points should not be inferred from the offense labels or from the existence of a pardon. The record’s “Corrupt Pardons” subcategory goes beyond the cited source because the DOJ list gives no evidence of a corrupt exchange or improper rationale; the proposed subcategory is therefore narrowed to “Presidential clemency.” This draft reports the documented clemency and conviction without asserting a motive.
